utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please sit down. Would the registrar introduce the accused, have him brought in? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Of course, as usual, I would like to greet friends, colleague interpreters, the court reporters. Once again, I wish a happy welcome to Judge Riad, who was away, and who will be pleased enough to notice that we still are sitting with the same witness. And we shall, without further ado have General Marin brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we go on with the cross-examination, let me ask the Prosecution how long they plan to take to complete the cross-examination. After all, we have to come to an end with it. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I think on behalf of all counsel, Judge Riad, welcome back. I do think, Mr. President, I will be able to complete this session this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's good news. I'm sure the witness will be pleased, too, because he has been on the spot for close to three weeks. And, thereafter, we shall ask whether the Defence wants to ask further questions in the framework of the redirect. Mr. Kehoe, I see that Mr. Dubuisson wants to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence is going to question the witness for an additional two or two-and-a-half hours, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, before my first question, I would like to show you a couple of documents. Mr. Dubuisson, and I would like to show the Brigadier Defence Exhibit 373, and then Prosecution Exhibit 387.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, if I may, Defence Exhibit 373 is a document that we discussed previously dated the 21st of June 1993 at 2015 hours, and this is the order signed by Colonel Blaskic forbidding using prisoners of war to dig trenches, and I refer you specifically to paragraphs 1 and 2. Mr. President, I don't think this document is showing up on the ELMO. Gentlemen? There it is, thank you. The next document, or that document that we just talked about, the Defence document, is Defence 373, dated 21 June, 1993. And let me read to you a paragraph in Prosecution document in 387, which is a report of then Lieutenant Colonel now Brigadier Alastair Duncan of the Prince of Wales own Regiment of Yorkshire. I realise there is no BCS translation; however, if we could put page 4 of that document on the front page of the ELMO. Yes, please. Push it up a little bit. Number 4 had to do with the release of the prisoners. "Ambassador Thibault thanked all for their assistance with the release of prisoners. It was agreed that: a) all would support the future activities of ICRC and the work of the Joint Commission; and b) if not already issued, commanders were to issue precise orders on the treatment of prisoners and the punishment of those commanders who disobeyed these orders. Commanders who disobeyed these orders were to be removed from command. Specific orders were to be issued forbidding prisoners being asked or made to dig trenches." Now, Brigadier, both of these documents obviously are executed on the same day, and the order of Colonel Blaskic was at 2015 on the evening of the 21st. Is it clear to you, as Chief of Operations, Brigadier, that it was based on the agreement in this meeting that Colonel Blaskic issued this order, Defence Exhibit 373, specifically forbidding the use of prisoners of war to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The order is issued by the commander, this is a Defence Exhibit, and this was signed for the General by Franjo Nakic, and it was written by Mr. Totic. And I see the date when it was created, the 12th, but in the report of the representative of the UN, I do not see the date when this document was created. So, would it be possible for me to see the date when this document was created? And why am I asking about this? Because there were also the January conflicts and then the commissions worked on that, too; that is, on the release of prisoners, and then there were the April conflicts, and these were the conflicts in June. That is to say, when the army made an all out attack on the units of the HVO. If it would be possible for me to see the date, then I could give you a precise answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Brigadier, let me just correct one error that you made, probably overlooked it. The document that was signed by Franjo Nakic on behalf of Colonel Blaskic was 21 June 1993; was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the document that was created at the time when the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried out an all out attack against the units of HVO, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Zepce, Fojnica, Kakanj; in that area there was fighting and there were prisoners of war on both sides, and it is certain that this was done in order to avoid making the same mistakes that were made until then towards civilians and prisoners of war. That is why General Blaskic then issued such orders preventing all possible illegal attacks and such treatment of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if we could put Prosecution 387 back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read the top of this report, and it is dated 21 June, 1993, Brigadier. It says "Second meeting of the Joint Command, 21 June, 1993, record of decisions." And it is in that particular document in paragraph 4 where specific orders were to be issued forbidding prisoners being asked or made to dig trenches. So my question for you again is: It's clear to you, as the Chief of Operations, that this order forbidding the digging of trenches took place on the same day as this meeting, and the order was issued pursuant to the agreement made in this meeting; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the date on the document of the United Nations, and the date on the document of General Blaskic confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: It was pursuant to the agreement at that meeting that Blaskic authorised the order to be issued forbidding the digging of trenches by prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the logic of things, that is the conclusion that may be drawn. However, one cannot see that on the basis of General Blaskic's document that it was made because of that meeting. This document of General Blaskic invokes the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. Since I was not the author of the document, I did not sign it, and I cannot say for sure whether it came as a result of the agreement reached at the meeting you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, once again, you received a copy of this; did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The copy of General Blaskic's orders?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it came to the operations department and I remember, I said that I remember the document. But I'm not the author of the document, and it says here on the basis of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions of such and such a date, and on the basis of these provisions, this order is being issued. And I said under which conditions it was created, because then the fighting spread throughout Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, again, you were the Chief of Operations at this time. Was this order discussed by Blaskic at morning briefings with members of the staff, including you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time the head of staff was at the briefings, and he attended the meeting of General Blaskic's. At that time when the head of the staff was at briefings, I was not at briefings; but I am familiar with this order, and I'm familiar with the subject matter involved, and I know what the intention was. The intention was to treat prisoners of war and civilians properly. That was the main objective of this document, and it is quite clearly shown by the document itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we will move on to another subject, and I would like to go back to the investigation of Ahmici by SIS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are going to come back to the investigation in Ahmici, but haven't you dealt with this already? You know, after all, we can't come back to this indefinitely, remember the time we took on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's just a couple of questions concerning the chain of command and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I know, but you know, you're talking about a couple of questions, five or six. I don't agree, Ahmici has been dealt with, whether you like the answers you got or not. So, you can ask one question, but I don't know how much time we're going to devote to this. This is time taken from the Defence time. So, you can put the question, but don't overdo it. We don't want to spend too much time on Ahmici. I think we have dealt with this enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I understand. I don't know, Counsel, if you have a question in this regard or a statement to issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: First of all, let us hear the question, and then perhaps we are going to have some suggestions, and we might not, on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, can I have Defence Exhibit 251 put on the ELMO, please, which is this document here? Mr. President, I'm not going into the facts and the details of Ahmici, I'm just relating to this particular flow chart; so, have no fear, we won't be asking questions with regard to the events in Ahmici as we did last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's easy, if you ask too many questions, I will stop you. I have no fear. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is a document that you introduced into evidence during your direct testimony. Can you see that okay, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document that represents the organisational structure of the Croatian Defence council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it would be a good thing if the witness got a document, because you can't really read from the screen, the letters are too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the entity that was given the authority to investigate Ahmici was SIS, and SIS was a counter intelligence and a security agency; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The security service did not have the authority to investigate this. But the commander of the Operative Zone issued orders to that effect. And why, I already mentioned that, because the commander of the Operative Zone could not get sufficient information on this. So that is why he issued orders to the security forces to investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it is a counter-intelligence and security agency. And my question for you, with regard to the box that we have in Central Bosnia, the person that is responsible for SIS in Central Bosnia was Anto Sliskovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person in charge of the security and information service, that is to say, to the extent to which it was organised in the Operative Zone, Anto Sliskovic was assistant commander for security matters. I am not aware of whether there was another service in addition to this one which dealt with civilian security. I cannot speak of that for sure, because I'm not familiar with these matters. But I know that in the command of the Operative Zone there was an assistant in charge of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence suggests that we move to closed session just for a minute, please, for all the reasons that we mentioned time and again last week. Private session will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I will go for the latter solution (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question for you, Brigadier, if we go back to the transcript, was how often did they come into Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall try to remember and give you a figure. From April until the Washington Accords, I don't think there were more than 12 or 13 flights. I'm not sure, but that is the approximate figure. So I cannot explain the word "often" or "frequently". That would mean three times a week, but that's certainly not the case because it was simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the reporter who was talking during that interview stated that the flights came in daily, your testimony is that that reporter would be incorrect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That journalist was certainly wrong, and that is what UNPROFOR knows, and that is what all of us up there knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, when did these flights, these helicopter flights, begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said after the Lasva Valley was almost completely cut off, and when practically all the roads leading there were blocked. I shall try to remember. It is possible that the first helicopter arrived in August 1993. I really cannot confirm a date now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you another exhibit. Mr. Usher, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 533.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, Exhibit 533, the map that you have before you, is a portion of Exhibit 216, a map of Busovaca. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photograph is quite unclear, and I cannot confirm by anything that this is exactly Busovaca. However, some buildings perhaps show that this might be the municipality and town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we can clarify it for you, Brigadier. Mr. Dubuisson, do you have Exhibit 216 handy? If you don't, we can move on. Exhibit 216 is a large -- the large overhead of this particular document from which this smaller map was extracted. If not, we'll move on and show it to the Brigadier after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I don't think I have it right now, but I'm going to check. No. It is presently in the vault, so I can't give it to you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, just take a look at that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That particular circle in the area, and I will tell you as a reference point, is the football pitch or football field in Busovaca. Now, the HVO, and you as Chief of Operations, did the HVO have helicopter flights coming in and out of Busovaca, and did they land on the football field in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the war, that is to say in the month of August, as far as I can remember, when the helicopters were carrying out the tasks that I mentioned, that is to say the transportation of the wounded, and also a smaller part of logistic supplies because it was impossible to do more than that due to the lack of space in the Lasva Valley --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You've already said that. You've already answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I know, but you told us what the helicopters were there for, for logistics, for evacuation. So please do answer the question put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I shall give a comprehensive answer, so just two sentences really. Because of that situation, the helicopters changed the place where they would land. Why? Because if they would land in one place and the units of the BH army, all of this was quite visible, they would notice this and then they would shell that particular point. So sometimes the helicopter would land at the area that we saw on the picture, and sometimes they would land in Busovaca at a given location. I'm not sure that during the war it could have landed on the stadium -- football field, but with the same task and with the same intention that is why they arrived. So sometimes the helicopters would land on the territory of Vitez and sometimes on the territory of Busovaca, but for the reason I explained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Let's move to Prosecution Exhibit 433/6, and for reference, this is a photograph taken by Captain Lee Whitworth and it has to do with a medivac excursion where bodies, wounded were taken from the Kiseljak area to areas down in Croatia. It should be this one, Mr. Dubuisson. Yes, that's the one. Now, Brigadier, just for the sake of clarity, this is a photograph that was introduced in evidence by an officer, a former officer of the British battalion concerning a medivac execution where the wounded were taken from Kiseljak to get some assistance, I believe, down on the Dalmatian coast, and he testified that this particular helicopter flight took off and landed from Kiseljak, again on the football field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this and I cannot deny it, because Kiseljak was cut off from us. Whether the helicopter landed on the football field or not, that I'm not aware of, but I remember a medical evacuation in which my late mother was evacuated too, because it was impossible to give people medical treatment there at all, and then UNPROFOR did us a favour and transported these people to Kiseljak. And then I don't know exactly how these civilian patients were transported after that by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as you know, helicopter flights took off and landed in Busovaca and Vitez. Brigadier, you testified that Colonel Blaskic did not leave the Vitez pocket until after the Washington Accords, which I believe was signed the last week of February or the first week of March of 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness did not say that. The witness said that Blaskic did not go to Kiseljak. He did not say that he did not leave the Busovaca Vitez pocket. He simply said he did not go to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Blaskic leave the Vitez pocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic did not go to Kiseljak. But as far as I can remember, in October or November, 1993, he flew, at the invitation of the head of the Main Staff, somewhere to Herzegovina to Posusje or Mostar, and then he returned three or four days later. That is the only day, or rather the only time that I remember General Blaskic left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Blaskic took a helicopter flight from Vitez to Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was in October or November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do it any other time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never again until the accords were sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the accords were signed in, on the 1st of March of 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Washington Accords, if that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Washington Accords, 1 March 1994. Let me show you Prosecution Exhibit 356, excuse me, 456/114. Now, Brigadier, I show you Prosecution Exhibit 456/114 dated the 4th of February 1994 at 10.00 in the morning, and it is sent to the Chief of Staff, HVO main headquarters, specifically Lieutenant General Ante Roso. Take a look at this document, Brigadier, and focus on number 2. It says on number 2, "Please send the automatic rifles and machine guns which I previously requested during my stay, as they are absolutely necessary." Now, that document reflects, does it not, that Blaskic was out of the Vitez pocket and down in the Mostar area sometime around the 4th of February, or before the 4th of February, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the time that I refer to, the end of October or beginning of November, that is what I said. General Blaskic, at the end of October or the beginning of November was at the Main Staff. The problem of logistics and these needs is not a daily problem, it is something we had to deal with every day throughout the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date of the order that is before you, Prosecution Exhibit 456/114?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of me is a request for providing the logistics equipment mentioned in this document. So, that is a request towards, addressed to a superior. General Blaskic is asking the head of the Main Staff to send this equipment. I remember when it arrived, it was thrown out of helicopters, and part of it also went to the territory under BH army control. So, practically we were deprived of part of this equipment. I am particularly referring to boots, winter uniform, socks and underwear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date of this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date of this request is the 4th of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 4th of February of 1994. Would that indicate to you, Brigadier, that Blaskic had been down in the Mostar area another time, beyond the time that you mentioned to us in October or November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said about this time when he went there. I am not aware of any other departures of his, but I claim that he did not leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, would you agree with me that based on the request that you have before you, it would appear that Blaskic made another trip to the Mostar area, other than the one that you mentioned in October or November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness answered twice, and the claim that my distinguished colleague, the Prosecutor, keeps repeating does not stem from this document. It simply says that Blaskic had previously requested automatic weapons, automatic rifles, so such a claim does not stem from this document, and the witness already replied to this twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you forgive me, with all due respect, I don't quite agree with you in the way you explain matters. Indeed, I believe that this document is not a fundamental contradiction of what your witness stated, but obviously between November and February you have got three months that elapsed; and according to the style of this document, it can be seen it is not a style showing that a lot of time has gone by. I don't think it is an illegitimate question. You are asking for armed guns, and that I already asked during my stay; it could easily be imagined that I have asked you for rifles a number times. And so, it's quite a legitimate question, I would like the witness to try and answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect, I suggest that we have this paragraph precisely translated. Perhaps my English is not good enough, but in my language it says not "stays" in the plural, but "stay" in the singular. So, could we please have a look at the original text? I can read it, or the Brigadier can read it, it's all the same, and then the Court interpreters can interpret it again. So it is not "visits" in the plural, but in the singular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, could you please read out paragraph 2, which indeed casts a doubt as to whether the accused alludes, first hypothesis to the November stay, or whether he possibly might allude to another stay. Could you please tell us the second paragraph, please send us --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. So, I'm reading the second paragraph. INTERPRETER: Interpreters do not have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could put the BCS copy on the ELMO so the interpreters can read it, I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, once again, I shall try to read point 2. "Please send automatic rifles which I requested during my stay, as well as machine guns, because they are indispensable to us."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, there is no contradiction between the translation I have here in my hands and the one I've just heard, so the question remains legitimate. It could be understood as follows: If it is a stay later than November, you could have a much more commanding style. It could be said, "I've been here, it's three months since I've been here, full in the middle of winter, we need that," so, it could be a different style. Please try and answer the question, Brigadier. I shall put the question to you, if you don't mind. On the basis of the translation you've just heard, do you maintain that when the accused said, I quote, "in my stay", the only possible stay is the November stay; or do you think that there were possibly other stays, given the way and the style of the sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I am referring to the stay in the month of November. There were no other stays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's stay with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you remain on the same topic, Mr. Kehoe? We're going to have a long afternoon, we could have a 10 to 15-minute break; are you finished with this item?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I wanted to ask the Brigadier a couple of questions about this flight down in November, but I can wait until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In war time, can a general wait for three months before he reminds or asks one of the subordinates to have one of his orders executed? Is that a normal case in war time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, requests for logistics addressed to the Main Staff went continuously, month after month. If we look at some other reports there were also some requests, because logistics for the units of the HVO in Central Bosnia, which were completely, for HVO units there, they were completely surrounded, it was a question of to be or not to be. If we did not get minimum requirements we could not defend ourselves. So this is not one single request I'm talking about, there were constant requests. They were in daily operative reports, there was requests for logistics all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we need a break, we can do with a break, it's good for the interpreters, it is going to be a long afternoon. We shall have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the photograph that's up on the easel to your right and behind you is photograph 216; does that give you a better view of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does, that is the photograph that I had on the ELMO, on the screen, the one that I saw. I looked at it, I analysed it, and along here, and this main road, I think that this is, in fact, Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I just wanted to give you an opportunity to look at the entire photograph in fairness before, as reference back to Prosecution Exhibit 533.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, let me ask you just one or two questions about this helicopter flight by Blaskic in October or November of 1993, I think you said November. Who else went with Blaskic to the Mostar area in this helicopter flight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, from the Operative Zone headquarters, General Blaskic went and one or two members of his personal security. And during General Blaskic's stay with the head of the Main Staff, he was replaced by somebody who is today a general, and he was Colonel Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else went in the helicopter with Blaskic? Who were the other officers, or who else from his staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was nobody from the other officers from the staff of the Operative Zone in the flight in which General Blaskic was on, at least not from my department. I know it was not the head of the Main Staff, and as far as I recall, nobody went with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, was this an HV helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I recall, the HV, during the war, had two helicopters, which it has today. I think that they are transport ME 8 helicopters. And in the Army of the Federation, the Croatian component has these two helicopters which were used in the war, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, who owned the helicopter that Blaskic travelled in to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO, that is to say the HVO, the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, when Blaskic went to Mostar, who did he meet with; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, but I suppose that he went to the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did he meet with HV members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, at this time, to your knowledge, was there contact between the HV and the HVO? And I'm talking about during 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I do know that there were no contacts between the command of the Operative Zone and the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, at that time in 1993, was Blaskic, as well as yourself, were you citizens of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, that is to say, at that time, I was, I had citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and therefore, I was a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina; whereas afterwards, after the end of the war, when the Republic of Croatia, by virtue of its constitution gave guarantees for all Croats living wherever they may be living, if they should so desire, can take Croatian citizenship, I took that Croatian citizenship, and I now have dual citizenship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, are you travelling on a passport of the Republic of Croatia right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a free citizen, yes, I have a Croatian passport. When I travel in the name of the Army of the Federation, while the old passports existed of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then we travelled with the Bosnia-Herzegovina passports. Now, as far as I know, there is a phase by which unified passports are being published for all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is information which is outside the scope of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One clarifying question on this helicopter. What kind of HVO helicopter was it? Pardon me if I didn't get that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember now, it was a ME 8, I think it is a Russian helicopter, a transport helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, in flying down to the Mostar area, did Blaskic fly over Serb held territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the corridor, the corridor of the flight from Posusje to Herzegovina to Central Bosnia, as far as I recall, was via Mount Vranica. And that territory was controlled by the BH army, and the wounded were transported via that corridor, those wounded which were taken away by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us previously, and this is at page 13485, that "during 1993, when Kiseljak, in the area around Kiseljak was fully surrounded, according to the information that I had at the time, that is to say, for the purposes of logistics and supplies, the HVO did co-operate with the Republika Srpska with regard to this matter." So in 1993 there was some co-operation that you discussed in the Kiseljak area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kehoe, but let the witness react.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Because, it was a very long examination-in-chief, and it can be understandable if the witness needs some time to recollect the information in relation to the question asked. Do you remember that time which was just quoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I remember what I said. The information that was generally given contains, amongst the population, the soldiers, that is to say, that there was co-operation between, that is to say the units, the HVO Kiseljak and the Army of the Republika Srpska, in connection with logistics for that enclave. To what extent, what time and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that you had an accurate recollection of that quotation made by the Prosecutor. Do ask the question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you noted that the Serbs were cooperating with the HVO in the Kiseljak area. Was Blaskic cooperating with the Serb army that was stationed on the Vlasic Mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Blaskic never co-operated with the Army of the Republika Srpska. And the HVO units in the Lasva River Valley were, after full encirclement, were not capable of cooperating with the Army of the Republika Srpska. I have information from the book by General Alagic that after the encirclement and the fall of Travnik that the BiH army in the area of Neokrnja had co-operation, first of all, for logistic purposes and needs. Those are, that is the information that I have on the co-operation with the Army of the Republika Srpska. As far as I remember, and as far as I recall, and the information I came by during the war in 1993, on the war in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Alagic, talks, does he not, Brigadier, about Blaskic's contact with an officer of the Army of the Republika Srpska, the Bosnian-Serb army, and in their communications they had code names? Is that not what Alagic said, and Blaskic's code name was "the battery" and the Serb commander's code name was "the crank"? Isn't that what Alagic noted in his book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. What I said about General Alagic, I read that in his book, his book was published. I did not know in the war that that was so; but once I read the book, I have no reason not to believe it, if General Alagic said that he co-operated with the Serbs. Whereas, I do not have any information that General Blaskic co-operated with the Army of Republika Srpska, because that was practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I remind you that you were the number two in the chain of command, you were the Chief of Operations. This is no trivial information. Don't you have any personal recollection apart from that book you read? I mean, you were number two in the chain, you were Chief of Operations. This is no minor detail, is it? Could you try to provide an answer that would be not just what you can take from that book by General Alagic, no matter how interesting the book is? Could you try and answer the question put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. President. The question asked me, that is the answer that I gave. Now, if I'm directly asked whether General Blaskic co-operated, I will state what I know, and that is that he did not co-operate with the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the area that was around Zepce and Zavidovici was an area under the command of Blaskic; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area of Zepce was formerly under the command of General Blaskic. However, due to the fact that it was cut off, because it was cut off, severed, this area functioned in the same way as Kiseljak did, which means that we were not allowed to control it, we did not have an insight into the situation, and command over the units in Zepce was done by the commander of the Third Operative Group, General Lozanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, was the HVO cooperating with the Serbs in the Zepce and Zavidovici area, and were the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, helping the HVO transport prisoners down to prisons in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Co-operation between the Army of the Republika Srpska and the HVO in the Zepce area, I also know, as in Kiseljak, that there was co-operation in the area of logistics, because that was an enclave which had no other way out or any other way in receiving logistic support. On the transport and contents of that co-operation, outside the sphere of logistics, I have no information as to that or any knowledge on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you were the Chief of Operations, and now you are Brigadier in the Federation Army stationed in Mostar. Are you telling this Court that you know nothing about the transportation of Bosnian Muslim prisoners from the Zepce-Zavidovici area down through Serb held land into HVO prisons in places such as the Heliodrom? Are you telling this Court that you know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I truly know nothing about that, and I don't know whether that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about it? Did you hear that over 500 men were taken down in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hear of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear, Brigadier, that in addition to logistics in the Kiseljak area, that the Serbs actually shelled some Bosnian Muslim villages for the HVO forces in the Kiseljak area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, as far as you're concerned, Brigadier, you know nothing, other than what you've told us, about any active co-operation between the HVO and the VRS, other than the two incidents of logistics that you mentioned in Zepce and Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only remember that form of co-operation. Other forms of co-operation, I cannot recall, and I have no information or knowledge that there were forms of co-operation of that kind, apart from logistics co-operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, into August of 1993, Hotel Vitez, and you in the Hotel Vitez, and Blaskic as commander, you continued to stay in contact with the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In August, 1993, communications between the command of the Operative Zone and the Ban Jelacic Brigade evolved via, in the form of writing, that is to say, through reports and an exchange of information. However, due to the well-known problem with communications and links and the system, that is to say, it was not a safe and secure system, and technically speaking there was, the technical side of it was poor, so that contact of this kind and this kind of communication in writing was far less than it had been prior to the conflict with the BH army, correspondence was less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this communication begin again with the Ban Jelisic Brigade in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normal and full communication with the Ban Jelisic Brigade in Kiseljak, and with Zepce and all the enclaves began to function again after the Washington Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let me show you Defence Exhibit 254. Now, Brigadier, that is the document that you discussed during your direct-examination, and this comes from Major General Milivoje Petkovic. The date is 24 August, 1993, and it goes to Blaskic and Rajic. The document says: "Act urgently on the co-ordination regarding the group actions in the direction of Kiseljak and Busovaca. Execute mutual connections and consultations." That particular document clearly indicates, does it not, Brigadier, that Petkovic thought that Blaskic and Rajic could communicate; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not say that there was no communication whatsoever, and no correspondence. There was under the conditions that I stated, that is in reduced measure. It was made more difficult and it was incomplete, and General Petkovic, in writing this particular paper, had that in mind, and that is why he ordered this kind of activity as is stated in this particular document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we clearly have now established that there was communication between Vitez and Kiseljak. And my question for you, Brigadier, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No comment, please. You'll come to this later, won't you? We have all the time in the world for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One more thing, Mr. President. From what my learned friend the Prosecutor said, it would appear that only after this document was it ascertained that communication existed by packet link between Vitez and Kiseljak. However, the witness, when answering the first question, said there was communication but explained the kind of communication that existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, prior to your objection I made some observations in that direction to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I did not get interpretation of this, so I haven't managed to understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's move to Defence Exhibit 255, which is the interview that you discussed of Rajic from Slobodan Dalmacija of 7 December, 1995. I direct your attention to the particular area that was referenced by my learned colleague Mr. Nobilo with regard to the chain of command, and in it, in the interview, Rajic says, "In the beginning Blaskic was my superior, but later he transferred to Vitez while I remained in Kiseljak. Although Blaskic was formally my superior even then, the condition on the ground imposed a situation where he and I were equally responsible to the Main Staff of the HVO, he for his sector and I for mine." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't find that part, but I remember the substance when the Defence introduced this text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. If we could take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 380. You can continue to look while I pull out Prosecution Exhibit 380. Now, take a look on that particular document, sir. The second page, the left-hand column with the comment beginning, "Kresevo, Kiseljak," et cetera. Now, before we do that, sir, take a look in the lower right-hand corner. The newspaper reporter on this was a man by the name of Slobodan Lovrenovic. Do you see that in the lower right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. The name of Mr. Lovrenovic typed out here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lovrenovic, at this time, was the spokesman of the office of the president of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and his advisor on public relations; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know Mr. Lovrenovic. At the time when this document was created, I don't know which post he held. I never met him in my life, Mr. Lovrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a Slobodan Lovrenovic that held a post in Mate Boban's office, President Boban's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. "Let's just take a look at this one comment about Kresevo, Kiseljak and part of the Fojnica municipality also controlled by the HVO and also in Central Bosnia, but are not connected with the forces in Vitez and Busovaca, how are they holding up? Blaskic: It is certain that the will and determination of the Croatian people in these areas were awakened exceptionally early and have resulted in the firm defence of these areas. And I would add Vares here, which is in the structure of our second operative group in Central Bosnia. They are carrying out, in a co-ordinated and organised manner, all commands" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this document should be presented on the ELMO for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we put the English on the ELMO? I think it is on the ELMO. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "They are carrying out in a co-ordinated and organised manner all commands connected with the defence of the people and Croatian territories. This physical separation is not an essential or decisive factor, because we figured in our planning that the temporary physical separation of these areas could occur. Travnik is the first operative group, Kiseljak the second, Zepce the third, and Sarajevo the fourth of all the operative groups are under my command, and the chain of leadership and command functions absolutely, without interruption."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, that is contrary to the interview given by Mr. Rajic in 1995; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the opposite. Mr. President, Your Honours, I just want to say a few words about General Blaskic's interview. See, it was made on the 5th of October, 1993, at the time when in the area of the Lasva River Valley the fighting was very heavy and when it was a question of days as to whether we could defend ourselves or not. Under such conditions, for the purposes of promotion, for boosting morale, et cetera, any commander would speak affirmatively about the army that he commands. He will not say that he cannot find a way out of the situation, because if the commander says so, the army is going to leave the front-line immediately. Secondly, I said that formally, in the formal set-up, from an organisational point of view, the enclaves were within the command of the Operative Zone, but reality, on the ground, was such as Mr. Rajic had presented it. The reasons for that we have explained several times, and I'm just going to add another one; General Blaskic, from his position and from the point of view of his abilities, could not help Kiseljak or Zepce, because we didn't have enough logistics, we didn't have enough equipment at our disposal. The people who were in command in Kiseljak and in Zepce were left to their own resources, and they made their own decisions in keeping with this situation and the time when they were functioning. I understand this interview given by General Blaskic, as a professional soldier, in the way I described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have a lot of things to say, but I shall ask you to try and give very succinct answers, because I'd like the Prosecution to finish the cross-examination today. Do you have any questions relating to this contradiction between the two documents, or alleged contradictions, as you put them? Do you want to ask another question or do you want to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last question and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the bottom line is, Brigadier, is that what Colonel Blaskic told this reporter was not the truth. Is that right what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. General Blaskic was saying what the organisational set-up was, and Rajic described the situation on the ground. So that is where the basic difference lies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may, Brigadier, you said this document, and you can refer to it, the last two sentences, "All operative groups are under my command, and the chain of leadership and command functions absolutely, without interruption." That's what the document says; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says. If a commander would say, when being interviewed for a newspaper, that his chain of command was not functioning, that would be apart from any military logic, that he did not have control over the situation on the ground, and I told you the conditions were under which the document was created and what the situation was like that we found ourselves in at the time when this interview was given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, did he tell Milivoje Petkovic that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he told General Petkovic so, but Milivoje Petkovic certainly knew what the situation was and he certainly knew that General Blaskic could not influence the events in Zepce and Kiseljak. He certainly knew that as a soldier, because he was aware of what the situation was on the ground too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when this interview was given, the interview that is by Mr. Lovrenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present, and I first saw the text of this interview here in the Court. I repeat, we were in isolation, we did not receive any newspapers, and practically we were in a total blockade in terms of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you were in a total blockade and if you were in isolation, how did Mr. Lovrenovic get in there to talk to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where this interview was given. Perhaps it says so in the newspaper itself. Perhaps it says so here. The way in which journalists came and whether they came at all into the territory of the Lasva River Valley is something that I'm not aware of. If they came, regardless of what media houses they may have come from, they had to come with the assistance of UNPROFOR or other international organisations, because there was no other way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll move on to another subject, Mr. President. I'd like to talk to you, Brigadier, about the punishment and some of your testimony you gave on direct-examination about Blaskic's ability to punish and not punish. If I could, before we begin this questioning, with your assistance, Mr. Dubuisson, and the usher, if I could give the witness Prosecutor's Exhibit 38. Mr. President, I must say these are bound documents, so it may be difficult to put these on the ELMO. These are the Narodni lists, the actual statutes, so I don't know if it's going to be a workable solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this a new document, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, no. This was admitted very early in the case, at the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, when you get to tab 2, the Rules of Military Discipline -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, you were a Prosecutor -- you told us you were a Prosecutor in the military disciplinary courts. Now, the Rules of Military Discipline govern the conduct of the HVO, do they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I was Deputy Disciplinary Prosecutor, and that is what I was. We worked according to the code of conduct on military discipline in the HVO. That is the document on the basis of which we worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the military disciplinary court was located in Vitez; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The disciplinary court was established in the command of the Operative Zone, and officers in the command of the Operative Zone were there in, and if I remember correctly, this was August or September 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Operative Zone military disciplinary courts had the power to try members of the HVO and sometimes civilians within the Central Bosnian Operative Zone; didn't they? And I'll turn your attention to Article 52 of the Rules of Military Discipline, if I could, and read along with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which document are we talking about, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- correct myself. I don't know whether the military disciplinary court could prosecute civilians. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under certain circumstances, and we'll get to that, Brigadier. We are talking about the Rules of Military Discipline, Mr. President, and that should be tab 2. The first item I'm going to discuss is Article 52. Now, I'll turn your attention, Brigadier, to Article 52, subsection (2). Do you see that, sir, in the Rules of Military Discipline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which number is this document, please? Oh, just a minute. Article 52, "The first instance court of military discipline," is that it? Page 45?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, sir, page 45. It says: "First instance courts shall try the following individuals," and if we move down to Operative Zone in number 2, it says, “Operative Zone military disciplinary courts shall try non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of Brigadier--" "Operative Zone military disciplinary courts shall try non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of Brigadier in the units or institutions who are subordinate to the Operative Zone commander, or are in units or institutions within the area under the Operative Zone commander's authority, as well as non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of Brigadier serving in the administrative bodies of enterprises and other legal entities." Now, that gives the Operative Zone commander authority, through the military disciplinary courts, to charge and have tried people who are subordinate to the Operative Zone commander or units or institutions within the area under the Operative Zone commander's authority; doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says here quite clearly and accurately, and I'm going to try to explain this in the most succinct manner possible, in the Operative Zone there are units and institution, and it says here "institutions", and that is the logistics base and that is what it says here. So that is an institution. This text does not pertain to any civilians or civilian institutions at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Brigadier, but it refers to those troops that are subordinate to the Operative Zone commander, or units or institutions within the Operative Zone commander's area of authority; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but even more accurately, for units and institutions which are in the organisational structure and not those units which are being used operationally. So again, we're talking about brigades, the logistics base. That is what I mentioned in terms of structure. So that is what is being referred to, and that is what General Blaskic -- or, rather, the military disciplinary court could prosecute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't say that, does it, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand it that way, and I think it is said quite clearly. We should just go back to the organisation and structure of command in the Operative Zone when I spoke about the structure of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let's ask it very bluntly; the Vitezovi is a unit within the area under the Operative Zone commander's authority; isn't it -- aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in operative use, but I said that units that are under operative control -- command, the commander of the Operative Zone could not punish through disciplinary action, he could not appoint commanders, and other organisational matters related to that unit. I, as the head of the operations unit, never went to the Special Purposes Unit Vitezovi because this was not under our direct command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to intervene, because my distinguished colleague the Prosecutor is misleading the witness. In 52.2, it says quite clearly, in the second line, that the jurisdiction of the military disciplinary court pertains to military units which are subordinate to the commander, and institutions that are within the authority of the commander of the Operative Zone. So a distinction was made here between institutions that are on the territory of the Operative Zone on the one hand, and on the other hand, the units that are subordinate to the commander. My distinguished colleague read this as if this Article said that the jurisdiction of the disciplinary court pertained to the units that were on the territory of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nobilo can argue that all he wants, but what the translation of this is is that units that were within the area under the Operative Zone commander's authority, and there's no exception for the Vitezovi, there's no exception for Djuti, and there is no exception for the Military Police, albeit counsel would like that. There is no such exception in the statute. Now, we'll continue through the examination, and counsel can redirect on this particular point when he sees fit, but there are numerous areas to cover here and this is merely one of that many we need to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm reading from the original Croatian text, which is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, each to their own interpretation, but, Mr. Kehoe, I would like to let you finish your question, so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now -- thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move ahead, Brigadier, and let's talk about the two different types of discipline that the military discipline courts can impose, and let's turn to Articles 10 and 11, if you can flip back, and I think that should be on page 38. Now, in Article 10 deals with disciplinary errors and Article 11 deals with disciplinary offences; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, obviously disciplinary errors, based on this, can be punished with sanctions ranging from a warning to incarceration up to 30 days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about some of the documents that you introduced into evidence, and let's -- just for a sampling from 220 to -- Defence Exhibit 220 to 224, if you could just show those to the witness. While those documents are coming, Brigadier, let me direct your attention to Article 6, where the difference between disciplinary errors and offences is contrasted; do you see Article 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that reads that "Disciplinary errors shall be milder breaches of rules or other regulations in the performance of one's duties or in carrying out orders, as well as breaches of other enactments of authorised non-commissioned officers and officers, or a mild form of misconduct outside the service which is incompatible with the obligation and rights of members of the armed forces." The article then describes "Disciplinary offences shall be gross breaches of rules and other regulations in the performance of duty or gross neglect of important obligations and duties, as well as other irregularities and omissions of greater importance which have or could have serious consequences to the service." So just based on that, disciplinary errors which carry with it a penalty of disciplinary measures are for minor offences; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is what is written in Article 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at Defence Exhibits 220 through 224, and there are others that fall into this category, but briefly look at these. We will go through them quite quickly, we will not go through them one by one. These documents mete out or hand out disciplinary measures and are really for disciplinary errors committed by soldiers; aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the reports that I have before me, the disciplinary measures relate to soldiers within the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, and those particular disciplinary measures are, because they are in fact measures, are for disciplinary errors and fall into the minor category, and are not disciplinary offences; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to look at all the disciplinary measures stated here, but if we're dealing with imprisonment, with detention, yes, incarceration up to 30 days is a disciplinary error, according to this, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, briefly, can you go back to the Narodni List and go back to page 37 and look at Article 3, number 8; do you see that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading this text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that reads that "Any act by military personnel that contravenes the rules and orders issued by superior officers shall be considered a breach of military discipline," in particular, and there are numerous there, numerous items there, if you go to number 8, "all other illegal acts damaging to the reputation of the armed forces." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Article 8?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Article 3, subdivision 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 3, yes, subdivision 8, I see the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that includes in military discipline all acts damaging to the reputation of the armed forces; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says in line 8 of Article 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, would you agree with me that a commission of a war crime by an HVO member against a civilian population would be something that would damage the reputation of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not a legal man, as far as I know a war crime is a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a soldier, sir, and you assist in the military disciplinary courts, and going along those lines; would the burning of houses by HVO soldiers, burning of civilian houses by HVO soldiers, would that be something that would damage the reputation of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not only would it damage the reputation of the armed forces, but it is outside the code of military conduct. But I said that information of this kind, the names and surnames as to who the perpetrators were in Central Bosnia during the war, and even today, it was impossible to arrive at those names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would also agree with me, Brigadier, that forcing civilians to dig trenches or the destruction of sacral monuments; those type of things would also damage the reputation of the armed forces, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all those acts are outside the codes of conduct of an organised army, trench digging and all other events which occur, which have to do with damaging sacral buildings, are events which emanate from the times and the contents of war, that is to say, the war waged in Central Bosnia. Because what happened, happened in all three armies, in the HVO, in the army and in the Army of the Republika Srpska. However, I never justified them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, when Blaskic, as the commander of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, found out about a crime or found out about a breach of military discipline committed by a member of the HVO, he had the authority and the power to initiate an investigation; didn't he? And I can refer you to Article 59 if you want to review that before you answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you're reading 59, why don't you read 60, as well, and for that matter, 61, they all go together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you wish to ask a question related to 59?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just without reading the entire matter, I mean, Article 59 allows Blaskic, upon learning of a breach of the military discipline, to take all measures to secure evidence and to collect evidence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Article 59, the possibility for launching a disciplinary investigation and giving disciplinary sanctions is given to the commander of a company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's read 59, Brigadier. "As soon as a superior officer holding the post of company commander or other post corresponding to company commander, or higher, learns of a breach of discipline committed by a subordinate, he shall undertake all necessary measures to secure evidence and collect information relevant to establishing the facts and inform his superior officer accordingly." So, clearly from a company commander, Blaskic is higher, Blaskic has the power to order that evidence be secured and order that evidence be collected; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to order the implementation of this activity to the commander of a brigade, he will then go on down the line for a battalion and a company. And these measures were exercised by the commanders of brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at 60. In 60 Blaskic had the authority to initiate an investigation; didn't he? Read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Article 60 it states that a disciplinary hearing against officers and non-commissioned officers in the armed forces can be initiated by the officers and the commander of the brigade corresponding to the officers. So, this leaves the possibility of the first, the second and the third to do this. And at the level of the open active zone we did initiate disciplinary measures and procedure and disciplinary sanctions to the commanders of brigades and officers in the command of the battalions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't initiate any disciplinary proceedings on Ahmici; did you? Or any of the houses that were burned in and around the Vitez area; did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Disciplinary proceedings were not implemented in the cases you mentioned because we could not know the names of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you know when somebody disappears from a post, but you don't know when somebody burns a house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we do know, Mr. President, because that name is then sent from the commander of the brigade or whatever. But these events, when we're talking about criminal acts, the burning of houses, this was done clandestinely, secretly, and we cannot punish the commander of a brigade if he cannot arrive at the name. We saw the order of the 18th where General Blaskic ordered that all names be sent of all those who burned houses, mistreated civilians and so on. But no names were received in the command of the Operative Zone, because the commander was not able to arrive at the names. That is the problem, and that is the reality, and that is the situation, and the terrible situation that existed in the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's look at Defence Exhibit 468.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President if you want to take a break now or if I can move to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we might have a 15-minute break, but then when we resume our proceedings, you committed yourself to finish at 6.00; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm trying, Judge, I'm trying. I'm on my last area, to be honest with you, this is the last area of inquiry. I don't know how long this is going to take, but this is a rather significant and important area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What does the Defence think of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence is in a difficult position because it, we cannot continue to plan. Last week we had a witness in The Hague throughout the week and we had to return him to Bosnia-Herzegovina. At this point in time we don't know when we're going to begin, and under these circumstances, it is very difficult for us to plan our future work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to discuss with my fellow Judges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in, and the witness, as well. Oh, he is there, fine. Thank you, I'm sorry for that. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, the Judges have ruled or decided in this way: You can work until 6.00 this evening and tomorrow you will be granted another 30 minutes, not 31 minutes, but 30 minutes tomorrow morning. We shall resume our proceedings at 10.00 and you can work until 10.30 sharp. I shall interrupt you in the middle of a sentence just to have it finished. And I have the approval, it is a unanimous decision, I have the approval of my fellow Judges. Thereafter, depending on the Defence's wish and intentions, we shall tell them what we have decided; but the idea is that we should have everything finished with this witness by tomorrow evening. It's up to you to get organised in your questions, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm trying. I'll move quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's stay with this document, the Rules of Military Discipline, and sum up. Article 59 notes that Blaskic, upon learning of a breach, must take all measures to secure evidence and collect evidence; Article 60 gives Blaskic the power to initiate an investigation; and Article 61 gives him the power to appoint the investigator and state the length of the investigation. Let me show you two brief documents, if I can show you at once Prosecutor Exhibit 456/75 and Defence Exhibit 368.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have interpretation. I didn't have interpretation, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me review that again. Dealing with Article 59 through 61 of the Rules of Military Discipline. Article 59 gives Blaskic the power, upon learning of a breach, to take measures to secure evidence and collect evidence; Article 60 gives Blaskic the power to initiate an investigation; and Article 61 gives him the power to appoint an investigator and state the length of the investigation. Now, I would like to direct your attention to a couple of documents, 456/75 and Defence 368. Take a look at this first exhibit, Exhibit 456/75 of 4 September 1992. And in this order Blaskic is seeking information on a man by the name of Mladen Cosic; is he not? Tells them to arrest him and take him to prison. And number 2, he says, "Prepare all necessary documents for the above-named, as well as the evidence to support the charges of vandalising premises in the Kiseljak police building and unlawfully entering the Kiseljak HVO barracks and abusing personnel while they are carrying out their duties." So in this particular order, Brigadier, he is ordering the regional military police to find Mladen Cosic, arrest him, take him to gaol and prepare an investigation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In this order, that is exactly all the tasks that are listed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Defence Exhibit 368, this is a document you discussed during the Defence case that is directed to the 4th Military Police. Blaskic has information that two members of the military police are expelling Muslims by force from homes, and Blaskic orders in number one to conduct an investigation and take disciplinary measures against the culprits; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It says here exactly the way you read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the deadline for that was 5 days later on June the 4th -- 5 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Blaskic did have the power, did he not, that in addition to disciplinary measures, he had the power to refer a case to the military prosecutor; didn't he, the district military prosecutor? And refer to, if I may, Article 29 of the Rules of Military Discipline. Let's read them quickly because now I have less than an hour. Article 29: "When an authorised officer establishes that a breach of military discipline is also a punishable act, the case shall be handed to an authorised prosecutor through channels. If it is in the interest of the service, the officer shall also undertake measures to initiate disciplinary proceedings. 2. When a violation of a military discipline represents a punishable act against the armed services which, pursuant to the penal code, is subject to a disciplinary proceeding, the superior shall transfer the case to the officer authorised to decide on the breach of discipline." So, in this case, Brigadier, if there is a breach of discipline, Blaskic has the authority to refer it to the military prosecutor; and if there is a crime, a punishable act, he must refer it, in addition to military discipline, as well. Isn't that right? There is a dual track here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the contents of Article 29 are concerned, I can add nothing more but what is said here. Now, for me to give legal interpretation, I'm not in a position to do so, because I haven't been trained legally. I can't say anything more than what it says here in Article 29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Let's turn our attention to Article 69 of the Rules of Military Discipline. That, read in conjunction with Article 29: Rule 69 says, "When a disciplinary offence has been committed in the course of a punishable action, the officer authorised to bring the offender before the military disciplinary court shall decide whether the service's special interests require that the offender also be brought before the military disciplinary court for disciplinary offence. If the service's interests do not require that the offender be brought before the military disciplinary court, the officer, as described in paragraph 1, shall suspend the military disciplinary proceeding and bring the punishable action to the authorised public Prosecutor."
