So, suffice it to say that if someone commits a crime in the HVO, Blaskic can refer it to military discipline and take disciplinary measures on that soldier; can't he? In other words, if someone is convicted of murder, and is convicted in the military disciplinary courts, Blaskic also can throw the person out of the HVO through the military disciplinary courts; can't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot clarify this any more than what Article 69 actually says. I can give an answer in terms of a specific case, in terms of the order that was given by the commander, in terms of 256; but what Article 69 says is what I can read out, too. I can apply it in a specific case, in practice. For me to give legal interpretation, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. President, it seems to me that this line of questioning, in my opinion, is pointless. This witness, who does not have any legal knowledge, is asked for the interpretation of a law. The law is self-explanatory. I really don't see why this witness should be reading this now and be giving legal interpretations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, the Defence witness already answered in similar terms, no need for you to repeat it. But I think that this question is relevant. Do not forget that the witnesses was the Deputy of the military prosecutor; therefore, he had some degree of knowledge and training, and he was to understand and know the rules. Was he not appointed? Did he not exert the function of Deputy of the military prosecutor? Did he not have functions in relation to the military prosecutor? I must have misheard something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the military prosecutor is a person who is a lawyer and who is in charge of proceedings, but the witness was involved in disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying, he had some function. He was appointed within the Blaskic staff, Blaskic was then Colonel, if I'm not mistaken, but the witness is going to answer himself. Did you or did you not exert the function of deputy to the military prosecutor? Or did I misunderstand something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, you understood me well. I was deputy military prosecutor. But what is this post? That is to say, if the prosecutor is not there, whose deputy I am, then I assume this role. But, Mr. President, just one more thing: In the military disciplinary court, there was a person who was a lawyer and whose job was to prepare everything for us. And we, as members, came there primarily because of the level of post that we had, and to judge it from a military point of view, but there was a legal person there who brought all of this together, all the things that the prosecutor is questioning me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to refute what my witness is saying. The military prosecutor is in charge of criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I've got an hour here, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would rather you correct the witness than correct the Judge, Mr. Nobilo. I would prefer you to correct your witness, rather than the Judge. So I did understand what the witness had said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. President, disciplinary, I'm sorry, it was a slip of the tongue. It was a disciplinary court and disciplinary prosecutor, I'm sorry, that is what it says here in writing, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, suffice it to say that if an event occurs, that particular event, committed by a HVO soldier, can be sent to the disciplinary court, Blaskic can refer it to the military prosecutor, or he can refer it to the military district courts; can't he? He can do all those things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In these provisions that you read to me, that is the way I understand it. However, in order to get to this situation, one has to have certain authority, in terms of pronouncing disciplinary action. Subordinate officers had that responsibility, too, that is to say, of a company, and of a brigade, too. So, that is to say, that if this, if an entire case would get to the level of commander of the Operative Zone, and if it would be in line with the contents that you are referring to, then it could be so, then the military prosecutor could take action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, let us talk about the other document on the first tab, which is the decree on the armed forces by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and we referred to these two provisions. It should be Tab 1 in that book right there. That's right. Turn to page 18 in that. Now, under appropriate circumstances, in N addition to the discipline of -- that we just talked about, the disciplinary courts, the military courts or the military prosecutor, Blaskic had the authority to relieve commanders, to appoint and dismiss commanders should he so desire; is that right? I refer you to Article 29, subdivision 7, and Article 34.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of these provisions that you refer to and in line with the authority vested in general Blaskic, that is to say, according to these rules, formally, legally, he did have the authority to appoint and dismiss certain commanders, but when appointment and dismissal of commanders are concerned, this was referred to to quite an extent before this court. The law was carried out in such a way that the commander, General Blaskic, could not, in reality, in practice, carry out all the responsibilities stemming from this provision. What happened in practice? General Blaskic had to be in a position to strike a balance, as it were, between the authority he had and the actual state of affairs in the place where he was. So in terms of this balance, there was, on the one hand, the authority of the municipal authorities, that is to say whether somebody could be the commander of a brigade or not. General Blaskic persevered and he wrote out orders based on these legal provisions, because in this way also he wished to set up the organisation and structure that was supposed to be there. However, as far as dismissal is concerned, that is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, based on the documents we've just read, upon learning that a member of the HVO committed a criminal offence or a serious breach of discipline, Blaskic had the power and authority to initiate an investigation, gather evidence, refer the matter to the district military prosecutor, refer the matter to the military disciplinary courts, relieve the offender of his command, and he also had the power to arrest him; isn't that right? He had all of those powers at his disposal; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm waiting for your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he had all those powers; did he not? He had the power to initiate an investigation. He had the power to collect evidence in the investigation. He had the power to appoint an investigator. He had the power to refer the matter to the military district prosecutor or the military district court. He had the power to refer to the military disciplinary court. He also had the power to relieve an offender of his command, and last but not least, the power he exercised somewhat freely, he had the power to arrest, order that somebody was arrested; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is exactly what it says in these regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's turn our attention to the rules of the military district court and Blaskic's obligation vis-à-vis the military district court, if I may. Now, I want to look at these documents in conjunction with the rules on military discipline, if we could. And if you could flip back with me for one amendment back to the Rules of Military Discipline, and I refer to you Article 59. Now, as we noted at the outset, Article 59 notes that upon learning of a breach, the commander such as Blaskic should take all measures to secure evidence and collect evidence. Let us look at that in conjunction with the document that is before you now, the rules on the military district courts, if we could, and I direct your attention to Article 27.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P534, 534A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at Article 27 on the decree on rules of -- district military court, and Article 27 reads as follows: "The commander of a military unit or military institution shall be required to undertake all measures at preventing the perpetrator of a criminal act, officially prosecuted, from hiding or fleeing lest the traces of the crime or the objects used in the process of committing it, which can serve as evidence, be lost. The commander is also required to collect all information that can be used in a criminal proceeding." So that is consistent with the Rules of Military Discipline that Blaskic, as the commander, has got responsibility to secure and collect evidence; isn't that right, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. General Blaskic asked his subordinates to give him proof about all events that pertain to breach of military discipline. However, we saw what he got; rather, that he did not get anything practically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let's go through exactly what we have at this juncture, and now, with that piece of information, I ask you again to refer back to the Rules of Military Discipline, and in Article 60, as it pertains to the military district court, Blaskic had an obligation, under certain circumstances, to initiate the investigation for military disciplinary courts; didn't he? Look at Article 60 on the Rules of Military Discipline. And continue down, and 61, again, we mention the fact that he had the power to appoint an investigator and determine the length of the investigation. And let us turn to Article 67, a particular document that we haven't discussed before, which notes that upon receiving the results of the investigation, Blaskic had the authority to have the offender brought before the military disciplinary court. And last but not least, on 94 and 95 of the Rules on Military Discipline, Blaskic was the one who supervised the work of the military district court and the Prosecutors; isn't that right? And I refer you to both of those.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Rules 94 and 95 of the Rules on Military Discipline. Take a look at those.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 94 mentions the military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about. I may have misspoke. I'm talking about the military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in addition to all the other powers that he had, Blaskic supervised the work of the military disciplinary courts and the Prosecutors in that court such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on top of that, when it comes to dealing with the district military courts, Blaskic, even though he wasn't directly involved in the military -- excuse me, in the district military courts, nonetheless had some obligations to arrest; didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says that it is so in these rules, and I'm going to tell you in practice something that I know was done. The district military court issued -- allowed General Blaskic to arrest some of the perpetrators of a criminal act, and had they authorised Blaskic to do so, I think that he would have done so, along with the Military Police, or in some other way had they authorised -- asked him to do so, he would have done so, or if they did not want to come peaceably, force would have been applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, Brigadier, as far as the military disciplinary courts went, Blaskic had the authority to arrest anybody he wanted; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot affirm that this is so, that he could have arrested anybody he wanted, I'm not a legal man, but if to arrest somebody if you do not have arguments that this is not in compliance with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me just talk for one moment, and we'll just digress for one second on the military disciplinary courts before we go back to Blaskic's power to arrest. And in one of exhibits -- and if I can show the witness Defence Exhibit 235. Now, you noted in this exhibit that the commander in Zepce was looking to have a military district prosecutor's office get involved with a number of criminal offences in that area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say so. As far as I recall, and I think that I remember correctly, I remember the document and my statement made to the Defence, I said that the assistant for information activities issue a request to be given additional information on the activities to move criminal -- disciplinary proceedings against the perpetrators or the offenders if a disciplinary error or offence has been committed. The reason he asked for this was that we were cut off, which means that we were not able to function properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, notwithstanding being cut off, the ability of the military district courts to operate in areas that were cut off was very effective; was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, but I personally think that it was not, and I do not know whether the military district court could have been effective, and whether it was effective in the Zepce area and the Kiseljak area. That organisation of the military district court is something that I do not know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let me show you a couple of documents, if I can have these marked, if I can. These are two documents dated the 10th of September, 1993, and the 29th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the document dated 29th of October, 1993, it will be marked 536. As to the document of the 10th of September, 1993, the document will be marked P535.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, take a look at these two documents. Now, Brigadier, these documents refer to the military -- excuse me, the district military court, and the first document, Exhibit 535, is an order of the 10th September, 1993, in the Vares municipality. Now, like Zepce, Vares was an enclave that was cut off; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at this. On the 10th of September, 1993, there is a request -- an order for temporary provisions of rooms. The order is given: "You are hereby ordered immediately to make available one courtroom and four empty rooms with the necessary furnishings, which will be used temporarily by the Chamber of the Travnik military district court based in Vares, and the deputy military district prosecutor." Now, this is signed by Anto Picinovic, is that right, with the -- and the seal? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I am looking at this document for the first time. I see it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Do you recognise that seal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With this stamp -- I did not have occasion to encounter this stamp in my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know Mr. Picinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the next document, 536, which is 29 October, 1993, again discussing the district military court. "Pursuant to the conclusion number, dated 20 August, 1993 of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, a Chamber of the district military court based in Vares was established and three Judges appointed. The Chamber began work on 10 September, 1993. In order for the Chamber to operate in conformity with the laws on criminal procedure, it is necessary to designate an official defence attorney for persons who are to be tried before this court." So pursuant to a decree on the 20th of August of 1993, a Chamber began work in Vares on the 10th of September of 1993 as this report reflects, dated the 29th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this document we cannot see whether the Chamber actually began work, whether the Court began work. It refers to a conclusion based on the Travnik district military court, et cetera, et cetera, and that it says it began work. I cannot say anything more than what is written in the text, and I said that the organisation, and location and actions of the district military court, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me, Brigadier, that this military court was set up very quickly after the decree was -- came down on the 20th of August. I mean, this Chamber started work on the 10th of September of 1993 in a place that was cut off from Vitez, such as Zepce was cut off from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm whether the court started -- whether it existed in Vares, whether it was in Zepce, because I have no information on that, because the district military court was outside the organisation of the army, and as far as I know, the military district court was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice, and the operative zone was within the jurisdiction of the Defence Ministry, which means that we did not have any organisational, or, I think, functional links with that particular court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know what time Your Honours are going to continue to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, you'll be given 30 minutes tomorrow, Mr. Kehoe. Does this question of the military court -- are you finished with it or you're about to finish it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to military district court, I'm finished it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, fine. We are going to put an end to this hearing, and we shall resume our work tomorrow morning, at 10.00 tomorrow morning. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
